paragraphs: It is tempting to imagine that the great oral epics were composed in a single act of genius and then, once written down, fixed forever. Evidence from living oral traditions suggests otherwise. Singers who perform long poems rarely memorize them word for word; instead they rebuild each performance from stock phrases and familiar scenes, so that no two renderings are identical. When a transcriber records one such performance, the resulting text preserves a single occasion rather than the poem as such. Scholars who treat that text as the authoritative version therefore risk giving a sample the status of a standard. A more accurate picture would regard the epic as the whole family of its performances, none of which has a claim to be the original.
